newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China Grains - Soybean markets quiet on CBOT jump.
newsitem.headline: China Grains - Soybean markets quiet on CBOT jump.

text.p: China's soybean markets were quiet as Chicago Board of Trade soybeans jumped out of reach of Chinese buyers, and Hong Kong traders shrugged off reports that China had bought a Panamax cargo of U.S. soybeans.
"There is no way China could buy at these levels," one trader said on Thursday.
China's feed suppliers were slashing prices, vying to attract buyers, grains and oilseeds traders said.
Chicago Board of Trade May soybean rose eight cts to US $8.83-1/2 on Wednesday, setting 8-1/2 year highs on perceptions that dry weather could cut Brazil's output.
Rumours circulated in U.S. markets that China had bought a Panamax cargo of U.S. soybeans.
China's feed meal prices have dropped by at least 10 percent since February as large domestic suppliers cut prices in an attempt to woo poultry and hog breeders.
"The feed meals are fighting for greater market share, so they lower the price of feedstuffs," one source said.
Simultaneously, demand was not very strong despite the onset of the March-June peak season for feed meal, a source said.
"It's really strange, domestic feed meal prices are stable, not much change, and corn has dipped, but international prices are going up," said one senior trader based in Hong Kong.
Sources said that weak sorghum and corn prices contributed to softer feed meal markets. Domestic prices of soybean meal were still around 2,800 yuan ($337) per tonne.
"I think China will be back in the (meal and bean) market in one or two months more," said one trader.
He noted that China's huge imports at the end of last year had satisfied short term demand.
Chinese buyers were also looking further down the year at new crop Argentinian corn
For soyoil, the price is acceptable at $565 per tonne, C&F.
